discoveries.explanation: Best guess: two stars eclipsing each other (an eclipsing binary). A dip of 18.319% repeats every 1.9904 days and lasts about 1.9 hours. Alternate dips have different depths (21.404% vs 14.691%, 714.1 sigma apart). A planet makes identical dips; two stars eclipsing each other usually do not, so the true period is likely 3.9807 days. This matches TIC 144539611 (TESS EB catalogue) on the TESS Eclipsing Binary catalogue (Prsa et al. 2022) (our period is half the listed one).

vetting.reason: Halfway round the orbit there is a faint 175 ppm dip at phase 0.41, small enough to be a planet passing behind its star.

vetting.name: size
vetting.reason: Dip depth 18.319% on a 0.91 R_sun star implies about 3.81 Jupiter radii (42.7 Earth radii). That is bigger than any known planet (limit 2 Jupiter radii), so it is too large to be a planet.

discoveries.explanation: Best guess: a stellar flare. The star brightened by 1.63% (26 times the noise), rising in about 12 minutes and fading over about 82 minutes. A fast rise and slower fade is the usual shape of a flare, a magnetic outburst on the star. Spacecraft glitches or a passing asteroid can look similar. We did not compare it with any flare list.
